entry.title: Study of Fluid POD Modes & Reconstruction

link.title: Study of Fluid POD Modes & Reconstruction

entry.content:
What we’re exploring

At the centre of fluid reconstruction, is decomposition of a matrix into feature components as describable smaller values and vectors. Classic examples of flow include a traveling Gaussian Vortex, which is a Gaussian blob shifting from left to right on a closed-loop. Another is an unsteady decaying flow or a Taylor-Green Vortex.

We’ll look at these two vortex types and analyse their Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) modes for information about flow structure, and how assumptions of the method arise in results.

Taylor-Green Vortices

Taylor-Green vortices make up a subset of vortex types defined by an unsteady flow decaying in time. It has an exact closed-form solution from incompressible Navier-Stokes.

Incompressibility gives the two vectors u, v to describe the flow, \(u = \partial_y \psi, \qquad v = -\partial_x \psi,\) \(\psi(x, y, t) = -\cos x \, \cos y \, e^{-2 \nu t},\) where \(\psi\) is the streamfunction and \(\nu\) is the kinematic viscosity. The vorticity, a measure of local spinning motion, is defined as, \(\omega = -2 \cos x \, \cos y \, e^{-2 \nu t}.\) Directional spiral flow can be recovered from the x and y components of the flow field in time.

Taking the Laplacian of the flow returns an inverse double, \(\nabla^2 \psi = -2 \psi \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \boxed{\omega = 2 \psi},\) \(\psi\) is then an eigenfunction of the Laplacian with eigenvalue \(-|\mathbf{k}|^2 = -2\) because it is built from a single wavevector \(\mathbf{k} = (1, 1)\).

Past this, we need to model the dissipation, which comes from the non-linear term self-annihilating. The 2D vorticity equation is, \(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial t} + J(\psi, \omega) = \nu \nabla^2 \omega, \qquad J(\psi, \omega) \equiv \partial_x \psi \, \partial_y \omega - \partial_y \psi \, \partial_x \omega,\) where \(J\) is the advection term, \(J(\psi, \omega) = \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \omega = 2 \, J(\psi, \psi) = 0\) because \(\omega = 2 \psi\), therefore a Jacobian of a function with itself. Which is where the nonlinear term self-annihilates, and where the closed-form solution exists.

Any flow with \(\omega = f(\psi)\) is a steady solution to Euler’s equations. Vorticity is constant along streamlines, so advection has nothing to transport. The viscosity is the component that drains the shape.

To model the slow decay, we use a heat equation, \(\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial t} = \nu \nabla^2 \omega = -2 \nu \omega \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \omega(t) = \omega_0 \, e^{-2 \nu t},\) decay is then a model of the viscosity and wavenumber. The flow decays at a rate proportional to the wavenumber. So a Laplacian eigenmode decaying exponentially.

We explore Taylor-Green because the nonlinearity vanishing leaves a linear equation, and that linear constant-coefficient equation on a periodic box has exactly separable solutions, one fixed spatial eigenfunction and one scalar in time. This is identical to the POD’s ansatz. Taylor-Green is not just a flow of rank-1, it is rank-1 because it has an exact solution. So the exact solution and POD-friendly are the same condition.

Traveling (Gaussian) Vortex

In contrast to Taylor-Green, a traveling vortex doesn’t have an exact solution, it is a kinematic field that is imposed and it breaks the ansatz. Motion for the traveling vortex is a literal translation of a 2D Gaussian through space. Fluid does not necessarily act this way, so choosing it checks whether it is possible and reconstructable.

This blob however is a steady Euler solution, a self-induced velocity that’s purely azimuthal, and \(\omega\) is constant on those circles. Which means it is spinning in place forever, which we’re putting in a uniform stream. Advection is then, \(U \cdot \nabla \omega, \quad \text{giving} \quad \omega(x - ct),\) a rigid translation. Motion is describable then as a vortex drifting in a background. But this too means viscosity is assumed zero, and a single positive blob carries non-zero net circulation, which no periodic 2D velocity field can produce.

By making this purely kinematic, it guarantees that every mode POD charges us is attributable to translation and nothing else. What will be visible from this generalises: convecting shear layers, wakes, rotating machinery, and others. The shape can vary, and the translation is what it costs.

Proper Orthogonal Decomposition

POD is not an eigendecomposition, it defines the single deterministic field \(\phi\) that the flow most resembles on average. It maximises the mean-square projection, \(\lambda = \frac{\big\langle |(\mathbf{u}, \phi)|^2 \big\rangle}{(\phi, \phi)}\) where \((\cdot, \cdot)\) is the spatial inner product and \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) averages over the ensemble. After writing the numerator out and taking the variation subject to \((\phi, \phi) = 1\), the stationarity gives, \(\int R(x, x') \, \phi(x') \, dx' = \lambda \, \phi(x).\) This derives the eigenproblem, and \(R\) (the two point correlation) is the only object POD sees.

POD is the unique expansion that is orthonormal in space and uncorrelated in time, which is how we’ll confirm the Fourier modes are POD modes rather than a basis that works. POD is also optimal for the best rank-r approximation in Frobenius norm. Which implies that the eigenvalues aren’t a summary statistic, they are the exact error curve, before you truncate.

Degeneracy means non-uniqueness, when eigenmodes are equal any rotation in eigenspace is a valid POD basis, therefore mode pairs are determined up to a phase. Symmetry overrides the data, if the ensemble is invariant under a group, then \(R\) commutes with that group and the eigenfunctions are irreducible representations; Fourier for translation, spherical harmonics for rotation, and Hermite for the quantum harmonic case. POD discovers nothing known with symmetry, which will be shown in the travelling-vortex case.

Flows are exact analytic solutions

Both flows are pinned to closed forms, and the referee gates them against those formulas directly rather than against a tolerance that would absorb modelling error. Taylor-Green is compared entry by entry against \(\cos x \sin y\, e^{-2\nu t}\) and \(-\sin x \cos y\, e^{-2\nu t}\) on the pinned grid, and the deviation comes back as exactly \(0.0\) against a gate of \(10^{-12}\). The traveling vortex is gated on its contract instead: shape \((4096, 128)\), every value non-negative, a peak of exactly \(1\) at \(t = 0\), and the relative spread of column sums held under \(10^{-9}\). That last one is mass conservation under translation, and it lands at \(6.3 \times 10^{-11}\), which is the grid aliasing floor rather than an error in the field.

Choosing exact flows is what makes the rest of the study readable. There is no modelling error anywhere in the data, so every discrepancy that appears later is attributable to the decomposition and nothing else. Taylor-Green satisfies the POD ansatz exactly and the traveling vortex violates it, and the contrast is clean because the data on both sides is beyond reproach.

The decomposition itself is held to the same standard. The method of snapshots is checked against an independent SVD on a seeded low-rank-plus-noise matrix, confirming \(\lambda_j = \sigma_j^2 / m\) to \(1.1 \times 10^{-15}\), and all-modes reconstruction plus mode orthonormality are gated at \(10^{-10}\) and come in at \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\). Everything downstream in the curriculum (gappy POD, sensor placement, SST) calls this same convention, so the plumbing being right is half of what the assignment is for.

Assumptions in POD

Every POD-based reduction writes the flow as

\[u(x, t) \approx \sum_{j=1}^{r} a_j(t)\, \phi_j(x),\]

and three assumptions are buried in that one line. None of them are assumptions about the flow; the flows are exact and assume nothing. They are assumptions in the representation.

Fixed Spatial Modes

The ansatz is separation of variables with spatially frozen modes. The shapes never move or deform, and all of the time dependence is squeezed into the scalar amplitudes \(a_j(t)\). Taylor-Green is that ansatz, exactly, with \(r = 1\). The traveling vortex cannot be written that way with any finite \(r\), because its spatial support changes with time and a fixed \(\phi_j(x)\) has no way of expressing “elsewhere now”. Modes are fixed in space, so we pay for trailing modes that fake the motion out of stationary shapes.

Linear Superposition

The state is assumed to lie near a flat subspace, not a curved manifold. Superposition with a constant \(\phi\) means a linear subspace, because the span of the \(\phi\)’s is flat by construction. POD returns the flat subspace minimising squared distance to the data, and \(\sum_{j > r} \lambda_j\) is literally how far the data sticks out of that best flat approximation, the equivalent of a linear fit.

The snapshots of the traveling vortex trace a closed one-dimensional loop in state space, and no low-dimensional plane hugs a loop. Taylor-Green traces a one-dimensional object too, but a straight line segment, which a one-dimensional subspace contains exactly. Both flows have one degree of freedom; only one of them is flat. POD measures the linear dimension and the physics carries the intrinsic dimension, and the gap between the two is the curvature.

Variance = Importance

The variance of the eigenvalues is assumed to equal the importance of the structure, but POD only ever sees a two-point correlation and nothing else. Everything invisible to second-order statistics is invisible to POD: higher moments, intermittency, and above all dynamics. A mode can be energetically negligible and dynamically decisive, and POD will rank it below noise, correctly by its own criterion and uselessly by ours. This assumption didn’t bite in this assignment, because both flows are single coherent structures, but it is the one that bites hardest on real data.

Centering Taylor-Green

Taylor-Green is rank one whether or not the mean is subtracted. The snapshot matrix is an outer product \(\phi(x,y)\, a(t)^T\), and centering only rescales \(a(t)\), so it changes the magnitude of \(\lambda_1\) without touching the rank. Uncentered, the leading mode carries \(\lambda_1 / E = 1 - 5.6 \times 10^{-16}\) of the energy, and centered it still carries essentially all of what is left.

What changes is the size of that share’s denominator. At \(\nu = 0.1\) and \(T = 2\), \(\lambda_1\) drops from \(793.676\) to \(10.763\), a factor of about 75, because the temporal mean of \(e^{-2\nu t}\) is not zero and most of the energy sits in the mean field rather than the fluctuation. The energy is conserved, not lost, and the budget closes exactly:

\[\underbrace{\|X\|_F^2 / m}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\|X_c\|_F^2 / m}_{\text{fluctuation}} + \underbrace{\|\bar{x}\|^2}_{\text{mean}}.\]

So the story that changes is not “one mode” becoming “many modes”, it is what the dominant mode means. Uncentered it carries essentially all the energy in the data; centered it carries all the energy in the 1.3% that actually varies. Energy fractions are meaningless without the absolute scale printed beside them.

Behaviour of Flow

Width Structure

Sweeping the blob width and plotting the eigenvalue spectrum on a log axis gives a fanning set of downward curves, one per width. Steeper curves are the wider blobs, which are spectrally narrow, and flatter curves are the narrower blobs, which are spectrally wide. Wide in space means narrow in wavenumber, which is exactly what the Fourier transform of a Gaussian demands.

The decay is governed by

\[\lambda_k \propto e^{-k^2 w^2},\]

so plotting \(\log \lambda_k\) against \(k^2\) straightens every curve into a line of slope \(-w^2\), and the blob width can be read straight off the fit. Inside its range of validity that law is not approximate. Measuring \(\lambda_{k=5} / \lambda_{k=2}\) against the predicted \(e^{-21 w^2}\) agrees to four significant figures at \(w = 0.1\), \(0.3\) and \(0.5\).

Both ends of the sweep fall outside that range, for different reasons. Blobs narrower than a grid cell are not resolved: at \(w = 0.1\) the blob is thinner than the spacing of \(0.098\), so the field is a single-cell spike and the tail of its spectrum is aliasing rather than physics. At the other end the periodic wrap stops being harmless. The wrap returns a periodic distance rather than a sum of periodic images, so once the blob is wide enough to reach the far side of the box it overlaps itself and leaves a kink at the antipode. At \(w = 1.9\) the field is still a quarter of its peak there, and the broadband content of that kink swamps everything: the measured ratio is \(2.9 \times 10^{-2}\) where the Gaussian law predicts \(1.2 \times 10^{-33}\). On a \(64^2\) grid the law holds cleanly for roughly \(0.3 \le w \le 0.8\), and the flat tails of the wide curves are measuring the discretisation rather than the blob.

Mode Pairs

The spectrum of a translating field descends in near-equal pairs, which shows up as a staircase with two points per step. The referee gates the leading pair at \(\lambda_2 / \lambda_1 \ge 0.999\) and measures \(1 - 8 \times 10^{-16}\), so the degeneracy is exact to machine precision rather than approximate. Each step is one Fourier wavenumber’s two-dimensional subspace, and the pairing holds for every wavenumber, not only the leading one.

Equal eigenvalues say the two modes carry the wave together. The quarter-period lag says their coefficients are the cosine and sine of the same phase: the circular cross-correlation of the normalised \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) peaks at \(1.0000\) at a lag of exactly \(n_t / 4\). Because the pair is degenerate, any orthonormal rotation within its plane is an equally valid POD basis, so the particular cosine/sine split is arbitrary and only the lag is a stable thing to test.

Vortices of Varied Speeds

With one blob, the speed changes nothing. \(T = 2\pi / c\) scales with the speed, so every run samples the same positions around the box and only the time labels on the columns differ, which POD never reads. The spectra for \(c = 0.5\) and \(c = 10\) agree to \(4 \times 10^{-16}\). The coefficients agree only up to a rotation inside the degenerate pair, so \(a_1\) comes out phase-shifted rather than overlaid, and the invariant is the phase-portrait circle, whose radius holds constant to \(1.4 \times 10^{-10}\).

With two blobs at different speeds in the same field, the wavenumbers interfere. Writing the field in Fourier shows that wavenumber \(m\) couples to wavenumber \(m’\) only when \(m’ = km\) or \(m = km’\), so a blob travelling \(k\) times faster ties each wavenumber to its \(k\)-th multiple. The covariance stops being diagonal in Fourier, the modes stop being pure Fourier, and POD returns hybrids instead.

The total is fixed regardless: the fluctuation energy of the two-blob field is exactly twice the single-blob field for every ratio tested, to twelve digits. What changes is the distribution. At \(k = 7\) and above the per-mode ratio is exactly \(2.0\) everywhere, because the resonant partner of each energetic mode sits out in the tail with nothing to trade. At \(k = 2\) the ratios run \(2.34\), \(1.32\), \(2.00\), \(1.30\): the modes satisfying the resonance condition gain and lose while the others stay untouched, and that redistribution is what the eigenvalue crossing looks like.

Fourier Reconstruction

Relation to POD

Over one full transit, the ensemble of snapshots is the blob at every position in the box, and that ensemble is translation-invariant. The correlation operator therefore commutes with translation, and the eigenfunctions of an operator commuting with translation are the Fourier modes. So for this flow the POD mode is exactly the Fourier mode, forced by the symmetry before the data gets a vote.

This is a general statement rather than a quirk of the problem: POD in a homogeneous direction on a periodic domain reduces to Fourier. POD is optimal, but being optimal doesn’t mean being good for the situation, and running it where a symmetry already exists is an expensive way to rediscover the FFT. It also explains why the discretisation is pinned the way it is: sampling exactly one transit with the endpoint excluded is what makes the sampled ensemble exactly translation-invariant, and including the endpoint would double-count a position and leave the degeneracy only approximate.

Expansion of Periodic Movement

Traveling a closed-loop 2D box means that the blob has a Fourier series. So coefficients are all that need computing.

Separating the space components as, \(g(x, y) = e^{-x^2 / 2w^2} \cdot e^{-(y - \pi)^2 / 2w^2},\) only the \(x\) factor gets transformed, therefore, \(\hat g_k = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int e^{-x^2 / 2w^2} \, e^{-ikx} \, dx.\) Completing the square, \(-\frac{x^2}{2w^2} - ikx = -\frac{1}{2w^2} \left(x^2 + 2ikw^2 x \right) = -\frac{(x + ikw^2)^2}{2w^2} - \frac{k^2 w^2}{2},\) and the shifted Gaussian integrates to \(w \sqrt{2 \pi}\), \(\hat g_k = \frac{w}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \, e^{-k^2 w^2 / 2} \;\equiv\; A_k.\) Therefore a Gaussian in \(x\) transforms to a Gaussian in \(k\), with the width inverted. Being wide in space means that the wavenumber is narrow. This is evident in the width-sweep results. Full field becomes, \(g(x, y) = \sum_k A_k \, G(y) \, e^{ikx}, \qquad G(y) = e^{-(y - \pi)^2 / 2w^2},\) where \(G(y)\) carries no \(k\) index. So every wavenumber has the same \(y\) profile, and only the amplitude distinguishes them.

Advecting the Gaussian

Advecting a Gaussian through space is defined by the shift theorem which states that a spatial or time-domain shift is a multiplication by a linear phase factor in the frequency domain. Which links the Fourier basis! If \(f\) has coefficients \(\hat f_k\), then for \(f(x-a)\), let \(u = x - a\), \(\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int f(x-a) e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int f(u) e^{-ik (u + a)} du = e^{-ika} \, \hat f_k.\) Translating multiplies each coefficient by a unit-modulus phase. Letting \(a = ct\), \(\omega(x, y, t) = \sum_k \underbrace{A_k G(y)}_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \underbrace{e^{-ikct}}_{\text{rotating}} \cdot e^{ikx},\) the modulus is frozen and only the argument moves, which splits the result in two: the eigenvalue depends on the amplitude, which the phase cannot touch, and the coefficient is the phase. In that wavenumber’s own plane, the state point circles the origin at radius \(|A_k|\) with angular rate \(kc\). Winding numbers enter here: pair \(k\) winds \(k\) times per transit.

Where Pairs Appear

Pairs appear as a consequence of physically plausible movement. The field is real, so forces \(\hat g_{-k} = \overline{\hat g_k}\), and sum over \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\) collapses into positive-negative pairs. In this example, \(g\) is real and even, so \(A_k\) is real and, \(A_k e^{ik(x-ct)} + A_{-k}e^{-ik(x-ct)} = 2A_k\cos\!\big(k(x - ct)\big),\) which expanding the cosine results in, \(2A_k\Big[\underbrace{\cos kct}_{a_{2k-1}}\underbrace{\cos kx \, G(y)}_{\phi_{2k-1}} + \underbrace{\sin kct}_{a_{2k}}\underbrace{\sin kx \, G(y)}_{\phi_{2k}}\Big],\) two spatial functions and one wavenumber. That’s forced because if you take the first term alone with the product identity, \(\cos kx \cos kct = \tfrac12\cos\big(k(x-ct)\big) + \tfrac12\cos\big(k(x+ct)\big),\) a single standing wave is two waves, one going each direction, pulsing in place and going nowhere. The second term supplies the same pair with the opposite sign, so adding them cancels the backward wave exactly and leaves pure forward motion. So the pair isn’t POD picking up on a symmetry in the data, it’s that no single spatially-fixed mode can translate anything. Motion in a fixed basis needs at least two modes in quadrature, per wavenumber. This is why the rank-2 truncation gets motion perfect, two is the exact budget for a travelling wave.

POD Modes

Spatially Orthonormal

Spatial orthonormality is the first of two defining properties of POD. On the interval, \([0, 2\pi]\), \(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\cos kx\cos k'x \, dx = \pi\delta_{kk'},\quad \int_0^{2\pi}\!\sin kx \sin k'x \, dx = \pi\delta_{kk'},\quad \int_0^{2\pi}\!\cos kx\sin k'x \, dx = 0.\) The last holds for all \(k, k’\) including \(k = k’\), which makes two members of a pair orthogonal to each other.

Every mode carries the factor \(G(y)\), so the \(y\) integral contributes one common constant \(\int G^2 dy\) that divides out in normalisation. Orthogonality is settled entirely in \(x\), and the shared \(y\)-profile means every mode normalises by the same number, so the ordering is governed by amplitude alone.

Temporally Uncorrelated Coefficients

Temporally uncorrelated coefficients are the second defining property of POD. It has the requirement that \(\langle a_i a_j \rangle = 0\) for \(i \neq j\), where the brackets average over snapshot columns and not a continuum. This makes it discrete. With \(\theta_j = 2\pi j / m\), \(\sum_{j=0}^{m-1} e^{i(k - k')\theta_j} = \frac{e^{i2\pi(k-k')} - 1}{e^{i2\pi(k-k')/m} - 1} = 0 \quad\text{unless } k \equiv k' \!\!\pmod m.\) The numerator vanishes because \(k - k’\) is an integer. This is the orthogonality of the \(m\)-th roots of unity, and it is exact in exact arithmetic rather than an approximation that improves with more samples.

But look at the condition that made it work: exactly \(m\) equally spaced points covering exactly one full period, with the endpoint excluded. Which is np.linspace(0, T, nt, endpoint=False) over T = 2 * np.pi / speed. Include the endpoint and one position is sampled twice, so the roots of unity are no longer complete, the geometric sum doesn’t telescope, cross-correlations leak, and the modes rotate away from Fourier.

Why These Two Make Them the POD Modes

Suppose you have any expansion \(u = \sum_j a_j \phi_j\) with \(\{\phi_j\}\) orthonormal and \(\langle a_i a_j \rangle = \lambda_i \delta_{ij} \). Form the correlation operator, \(R = \langle u \otimes u\rangle = \sum_{i,j}\langle a_i a_j\rangle \, \phi_i \otimes \phi_j = \sum_j \lambda_j \, \phi_j \otimes \phi_j,\) the cross terms die because of the second property, and what’s left is a spectral decomposition of \(R\). The spectral decomposition of a symmetric operator is unique up to rotation inside degenerate eigenspaces. So \(\phi_j\) are the eigenfunctions of \(R\), which is what POD modes are. From this, you can directly read off the eigenvalues: \(\lambda_j = \langle a_j^2\rangle\). Because \(\lambda_{2k-1} = \lambda_{2k}\), the eigenspace is 2D and the cos/sin split in it is arbitrary.

Reconstructed Traveling Vortex from POD Modes

The reconstruction is the mean field plus the retained modes weighted by their coefficients,

\[\hat{X} = \Phi_r A_r + \bar{x} \mathbb{1}^T,\]

and the mean term is not a small correction here. Averaged over a full transit the blob smears into a horizontal stripe at \(y = \pi\), which is a substantial piece of the field, so dropping it leaves a reconstruction oscillating around zero.

Sharper Features Living in Higher Modes

Each pair is one wavenumber, and \(k\) grows as you go down the spectrum, so the sharper features live in the higher modes. Rank two nails the motion and gets the shape badly wrong. Adding pairs narrows the peak and cancels the overshoot, which is the job the rest of the spectrum is doing.

Rank Feature Dominance

At \(w = 0.5\) the leading pair holds \(61\%\) of the fluctuation energy, and that \(61\%\) buys the motion and almost none of the shape. The reconstruction runs from \(-0.15\) to \(0.55\) against the truth’s \(0\) to \(1\): too wide, too smooth, and undershooting the peak by nearly half. A flow with one degree of freedom is being charged dozens of modes, and the first two of them are spent entirely on getting the blob into the right place.

Travelling Vortex Features

Negative Reconstruction

Rank two keeps only \(k = 1\), so the reconstruction is the mean stripe plus a single cosine in \(x\) with a travelling phase. A cosine has a negative half, and that negative half is the trough sitting half a box behind the reconstructed blob. It is not a glitch or a numerical failure but the exact optimal rank-two answer, and it is negative because we are truncating the Fourier series of a strictly positive function.

Mode Pairs

The pairs are why the motion survives truncation at all. A single mode is a standing wave and cannot translate; it takes two, in quadrature, to produce a travelling one. Truncating to one pair therefore keeps the translation perfectly intact while discarding everything that described the shape.

Descriptor Pairs

The phase-portrait circle is the state-space loop projected onto the plane spanned by \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\). So the animation and the phase portrait are the same object seen two ways, and what the rank-two reconstruction draws in physical space is exactly what that circle traces in mode coordinates. That is also why the motion comes out perfect: the projection onto the pair’s plane is a perfect circle, and everything the loop does outside that plane is the shape information that rank two throws away.
entry.summary: What the decomposition of fluids reveal about the reconstruction process, and how small cases reveal problems with methods in more complex scenarios.

entry.title: On Living Purposefully
entry.content:
Mortal Man ends with a question and no answer. Kendrick reads Tupac a poem, asks what he makes of it, and gets nothing back — just a name said twice into a room that was never there. That ending has been sitting in my head for a week, and it has pulled loose something I have been trying to say for a long time.

It isn’t a passing thought. It’s the culmination of an effort I have been putting in for years without having a name for it. In time it will be passing too — most things are — but I would like it written down first.

Living Purposefully

One of the most poignant lessons anyone comes across is the idea of living a purposeful life. I don’t mean this as a response against any system in particular, and I don’t mean anything revelatory. It is a response to existing: to choosing a path that takes your humanity on a road rather than foraging at its feet. Put another way, we can choose to grow complacent in the work and the environment we are placed in, or we can explore the parts of the world we are given and set ourselves up to cultivate the system we want to see supporting other people on their own journeys.

Mortal Man

The end of Mortal Man is a conversation, and it speaks to exactly where Kendrick Lamar is standing. He has faced reality and is searching for answers about the world to pass on to other people. At his most vulnerable moment his voice changes from what it has been across the rest of the record, and then he is overpowered by the voice of Tupac. What he does in that moment is open himself up, in awe of and in respect for someone who already walked the path he is in the middle of walking, so that he can hear that the world he wants to create is possible. Then he reveals the thoughts he has cultivated with the help of the people around him, in the form of the poem threaded through the whole album, the one that finally explains its title.

The theory in that poem is that a world gets cultivated by fighting your way to the surface; that once you are at the surface you flourish inside a system you built; and that after escaping the system that helped you succeed, you pass your lessons to the next generation — which is what Tupac should have been able to be for Kendrick. The song ends abruptly. Kendrick asks Tupac what he thinks of the theory and gets no response.

There is no response because the conversation is assembled out of an old interview Tupac gave to Mats Nileskär, a Swedish journalist who has spent his career documenting the story of African American artists. Weeks after that interview, Tupac was ambushed and shot five times in the lobby of Quad Recording Studios; he was killed two years later, at the pinnacle of his career, right as he was ready to show the world everything he had learnt. In Mortal Man, Kendrick takes over Nileskär’s side of the conversation, and because he believes he is standing where Tupac was standing then, the edited interview reads less like one person trying to understand the culture of another and more like two intellectuals thinking out loud at each other.

Tupac was where Kendrick had got to at that point in his life: hyper-reflective, ready to show the pimped-up butterfly he was about to become, after sowing his foundations in the opuses he kept making. His death forces Kendrick, who has now come up the same path Tupac walked, to pave the new path for everyone else. He is faced with being the person who lives purposefully after all that hardship. History has repeated itself here without an ending, and we are in the process of watching it develop.

It is a strange challenge when a work this impactful hits you at the right time and in the right place. There is nothing you can do with it except try to wrap your head around it, and that is where I am now. After a week of playing this album nonstop I am faced with myself. I felt I needed to explain myself — not to anyone or for anything, but for the same reason that I need to live a purposeful life.

I am in no position, unlike Kendrick or Tupac or people like them throughout history, to change the system to the degree they could. Even so, living purposefully is a lesson I am still battling with, still learning the nuance and the meaning of. The first challenge of living your own path is recognising where you are and getting yourself into a system that will support your growth. If no such system exists, creating one is a much bigger challenge, and one that most people never take on in their lives. “Firsts” are some of the most impressive people there are; they show you the world that can exist.

The System You Have to Live Inside

The next challenge is existing inside that system well enough to flourish in it. Retaining the inner beauty, the originality, and the core child that you are, while shaping yourself to fit the society that surrounds the people you want to be involved with — that is the challenge, and I have battled against it for as long as I can remember.

Barely a teenager when I moved countries, I spent my time trying to find the childhood I had just left inside the new people and systems in front of me. It was a losing battle, though that is only obvious to me in retrospect. Of course I was not going to find it there. Ever since, I have been swimming for the surface and wading through rushing rivers to work out what I was supposed to have learnt years ago. It made me hate the world I was living in — naturally — because it never showed me anything I wanted to see, and I kept demanding that it would. Even once I had accepted the system for what it was, I had no idea what questions I was supposed to ask, and I became ambivalent about the whole environment I was in.

What that period taught me is how flawed systems are, and it also taught me to be haughty about the first glimpse of reality I ever got. I thought I had cracked the code: systems are just flawed. The inherent flaws of a system are obvious when you study physics, because there the systems don’t claim to be anything more than what they are. That is exactly why they work, and the lesson was planted in me subconsciously through years of describing systems and examining behaviour inside them. Cracking those systems open revealed unnatural behaviour, and the ways the physics of the world actually works. A system teaches you reality by simplifying it, and that is the lesson that planted itself in my mind.

It wasn’t until I briefly read Either/Or by Søren Kierkegaard that the rest of it hit me. I had read a bit of philosophy by then, but I was not ready for Kierkegaard, and I don’t feel that I am now either. Even so, I still believe one core component of that book gets misunderstood. The text was, “…what was needed was someone who could, to everyone’s knowledge climb really deep down into the whole of mediation, mediocrity, and spiritlessness to plant there, for all to see, the explosive either/or.” People mostly attribute this to the meaninglessness of the contradictions that arise from sitting in exact mediocrity, which from that frame is what forces you to decide on either or.

I don’t believe that is necessarily the argument Kierkegaard means to explain. Taking the middle ground on bare connotations is meaningless, yes, but choosing to live between decisions is a choice to explore both sides, whether or not you come out of the exploration with an answer on either. You can choose to like or hate the system you exist inside, but if you are truly there to get the most out of it, you will stay ambivalent and extract meaning from both sides of the coin. There is no fault in the practice of not deciding. The key is recognising that holding a position on something is independent of your ability to choose between decisions when they matter. You don’t need a verdict on a system you both love and hate; it isn’t there to extract an opinion from you, it is there to teach you what you need to learn, and you can have your verdict later. In the interim, you don’t need to create your position — unless you are willing to exist in the limbo of Either/Or for the rest of your life.

Building the System

Systems are designed to support the people who recognise what they are and where their flaws are, because those people know the bounds. When you know the bounds of the system you are designing, you can choose to improve it or start your own from scratch.

To Pimp A Butterfly touches on exactly this. The world Kendrick exists in is one he fought to thrive within. By cocooning himself and working on his art and on himself, he thrived into the artist he is today, and he had to build the system of support that let him do it: creating music groups, developing his own art, using money to buy himself the freedom to keep going. Separating himself from society was partly to improve the art and partly to bring the lessons back to the people. By the end of Mortal Man we have met a man who used those systems to thrive and is now faced with building systems in uncharted territory, while beaten down by every challenge he faced along the way — challenges caused by the people who forced him into the beaten-down world he grew up in. He needed the chronology of the album to get his energy back before facing the next task, which is a much greater one. Being faced with that and continuing forward is impressive, and it is why the album hits as hard as it does, on top of the history of oppression, prejudice, genocide, and injustice behind it. Without people like Tupac to set the example, Kendrick and others might never have got to a world where they could express their art at all. And there will be another generation that gets to move on because of people like Kendrick. They need it the most, because of a history of injustice that most of us could not begin to comprehend, even though the genre of the life lesson is the same.

Where I Am, and Where the World Is

My journey is nowhere near as difficult as other people’s, but I want the clarity and the freedom I have to see my own position to be a means for other people to learn some of these lessons earlier than I did. It is only because I have the freedom to look at where I am without worrying about getting through each day that I get to have these thoughts at all. So these written words should all be taken as respect paid to the people who forged paths without the freedom to be.

Moving to the US was difficult, but a lot of that difficulty was caused by me. I was grappling for the means to find my home while being presented with a reality that wasn’t entirely mine, searching for the world that already existed while learning new customs — a force that showed up in every single interaction and every system in front of me. So what do you do, having not found the world you wanted to be in, but explore. I couldn’t escape the US, so of course I did what I could inside the world I was presented with: new hobbies, new studies, new careers, new sports.

The world was changing fast at the same time, and it felt hard to keep up. Social media and the steady improvement of its algorithms, rapid globalisation, a government permanently on the precipice of having the freedom to focus on the long-term issues it has yet to repair. Then, of course, the advance of AI, attention models and the improvements in LLMs. Everyone is being faced with new systems infiltrating spaces they thought they understood, and everyone is being forced to ask, over and over, how open-minded they actually are. I could recognise how open-minded I needed to be about the US and the environment I found there. I don’t believe most people have been forced to recognise their own level of open-mindedness, and I don’t think most people want to face that challenge.

What History Can Give You

When you are faced with a challenge of that sort, the best first action is to observe the past. The actions of historical figures shape the actions we choose to take on the issues that matter to us. My own journey of understanding was to search for meaning in the Stoics, with occasional detours into other philosophies. I read Plato’s The Republic, Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations, the Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu, Either/Or by Kierkegaard, and Beyond Good and Evil by Nietzsche (one of my least favourite texts). By far the one with the most profound impact was Meditations, probably for the same reason To Pimp A Butterfly has had such a strong one: it unfurled the chaos of self-reflection that had lain in me for the longest time. My natural tendency has always been to reflect on what I do, but philosophy gave me the means to think about it from a new perspective. What my path needed was someone who was living a meaningful life, a mentor who had decided to take the hard road. What Aurelius taught me — or more accurately showed me — is that choosing to live a life is an option. I had been beaten down by the world, mostly through my own immaturity, slowly forging a path, finishing undergrad, and then meeting reality. Observing that I had not actually been living, I realised I was a step behind and needed to step up: forget the hassles I was causing myself, learn to live a life, and then return the lessons I picked up along the way to anyone ready to help themselves.

Facing an unknown is the common link in all of these positions, and history only bridges the gap of getting to the original starting line. Life for me was wading through unnecessary noise to get back to a starting line that the people of the past had already made clear. Now, faced with all the challenges ahead, the best I can do is regain my energy before taking up the last little bit. History gives us the information that clears the 95th percentile mark — in other words, mastering the basics. I use that number specifically, because it also means most people are not even in a position to use the lessons the people of the past have given us. History is simply not enough for everyone.

Grounding My Own Reality

Seeking to forge my own path, I set about changing how I interacted with the world. I was working at a startup at the time — not the best situation, in short. Because I had been complacent about all the mishaps that came before, I wanted to help fix some of those difficulties. I worked to prove that I should be in a position to make decisions, and then did my best while I was there to make changes.

Another quick lesson I had to learn in that period is that you can give your best effort to your work, and when people won’t take the lesson after considerable effort on your part, you have to let it be and move on. There were changes I managed to make and changes I didn’t, and in the end the negatives outweighed the positives by enough that the arithmetic stopped adding up. Over the following while I cleaned out my workload and divided it between my fellow employees, and talked only briefly about my leaving — enough to give them the space to voice their own concerns without forcing my opinion about the decision onto them. Following its history without me, the startup improved for a short while after the hire I recommended, and then failed for exactly the issues I left over, though partly also because the employees realised they could move on and still forge their own “Berkeley startup story”.

Moving past industry and academia, I also wanted to affect the climbing world. Most people approach the sport with very little intent beyond the experience itself, which is a great thing on its own — the act of experiencing something and being present in it. But you occasionally come across people claiming they are ready to “try hard” or “get strong” with no perceptible effort towards either. It is such a plain and obvious lack of direction, and it is near-on impossible to get anyone out of that headspace. Climbing is really enjoyable, and it gets exponentially more fun the more effort you put into it. Experiencing that first-hand is what drew me into the sport and got me making clear decisions that push my goals forward. But I can’t serve only that purpose either; climbing hard on its own is too egotistical. I want to be at the top level to show people that it is attainable and not as far away as it looks. Every decision I make about my training is an attempt to be better so that other people can see they could do the same. A losing battle nonetheless, because I realise some people need to experience the exact lesson I’m aiming to get across first-hand before it means anything.

The Question Is Why

The key question I see people in these scenarios lacking is “why”. Considering it now, I understand that not everyone is geared to keep asking questions, because it frustrates them: it asks them to ask more of themselves. That is a jarring feeling, but the payoff is incredible. Asking yourself questions, and really judging yourself for who you are, makes you decide what you mean — the either/or of yourself. In the act of figuring yourself out, you keep finding more questions to ask about the world around you, and you get into this endless cycle of figuring out how things are connected, why they’re connected, what relations you haven’t yet thought of, and everything in between. Choosing to critique yourself makes the world more interesting and more beautiful, and in turn makes you a more interesting person.

Artists work this to the core, figuring out what makes them represent their meaning one way rather than another, and it forms the clear separation between a good artist and a bad one. There’s no reason this should be solely in the arts; every sector has its equivalent. I found mine in research, other people find theirs in business, or in law. Missing the importance of what you dedicate yourself towards is the gap most people leave when they try to live with meaning, because dedication only gives you dedication. The world is filled with so many other people — why not live a beautiful life and give that experience to them too? By choosing to live with intention you are actively learning, dedicating yourself to a shared lived experience, and handing down the lessons you learn along the way, voluntarily or involuntarily. Life is already hard enough even while we share our secrets towards improvement.

Losing Intention to the Machine

Lacking that intention in your life becomes critical when you are influenced by the LLM systems that surround us. You end up working towards goals outside your own, developing external preferences, needing constant approval for what you pursue. It becomes too easy to let someone take the reins, so why wouldn’t you — they seem to know a lot. Their judgement becomes the word of approval regardless of whether you had a thought of your own. People get, as they say, “lost in the sauce”, in this day and age. Losing yourself to all the flavours available from one substance. Getting lost in all the information and knowledge without the experience that binds you back to it. Without a reason to be pursuing your goals, they become ghost tasks, missing whatever it is that would make them the best they could be.

When I worked at that startup, the company seemed founded on a passion, and then slowly over time the goal shifted outside of anything that seemed worth pursuing. It felt as if the company was reading ideas off an LLM that sounded feasible but lacked the substance that made the company in the first place. Intention fell apart. Nobody knew what work they were supposed to be doing, because every idea was being pulled apart by AI into some subservient task. Once that process was underway, it became clear how much importance I wanted to place on defining my own future. I pulled away from AI for a while because of this, not because I believed it was a bad thing, but because I needed the clarity to see my own picture.

Re-learning How to Learn

During that time away, I had a major realisation of how much I lacked a passion outside of my hobbies. The job was very much a job, so I treated it as such: still putting in my best effort, but leaving it at that, with no ego or self-worth attached. That gave me space to explore novel research and try out ideas sitting at the edge of what I felt I could approach. It reminded me of my hobbies, pushing my abilities to the edge so that I can learn to deal with harder tasks in the future. A relief, seeing the reason I love my hobbies in areas I had only assumed would make a great career. What a feeling. I was concerned for a while that there wouldn’t be a field that spoke to me the way my hobbies do. So I dived head first, went to several research conferences, and tested out a lot of random and arguably dumb ideas.

Through all of it I was, and still am as of writing this, pursuing my master’s degree. The coursework hit a new high right as this was happening. Because of the workload before it, I had got used to understanding a task broadly and then deferring it to someone, or some AI, else. I had to learn not just to be interested in something, but to re-learn how to learn: to build the passion on the page, inside my own thought process. How to build a brain optimised to your interests.

Note-taking used to be my least favourite activity, probably due to a bias formed around teachers who would talk too fast, erase too fast, and work too fast. If you’re a teacher and you’re reading this, slow down; these kids need to process on their own without you giving them the answer. I still think a lot, though, because I was pushed to work that way. The ideas were floating around in my head but never reaching the page, because I was taught to be quiet and not to write much, since writing was too slow. And because I think a lot, words became my domain.

Taking Algorithms at the time helped enormously. I wrote and wrote and wrote so much. My notebook, which sat at around 2–3% filled for the entirety of the prior quarter, finished at 70% filled after Algorithms. It was in that process that I wrote down everything I thought and analysed how my brain worked around the subject: fine-tuning my questions to develop towards the goal, and thinking logically. Understanding how even a passing dumb question can lead you down a chain of thought that solves all the problems you’ve been having. Recently, the interconnected world of Dark Souls came back to me, and understanding a topic fits that exact theme perfectly.

Writing a lot is not the goal either. It meant I explained every aspect of my thought, and at some point that becomes too much. One time I spent four pages writing up a proof that could have taken a paragraph if I had just worked the problem from a task-first perspective rather than an all-avenues one. My writing had to be more structured and more task-driven, and that translated into my research, developing my writing towards the goals I wanted to achieve: pursuing tasks that meant something rather than dumping text and hoping the answer lives somewhere within it.

In essence, what I’m doing now is a clear example. I never wanted to explain to the casual person what was meant by living meaningfully; I wanted to know that experience and understand what I make of it. Randy Pausch would call that a “head fake”. Writing keeps gaining meaning when you have a purposeful task behind it, because then the writing itself becomes the task, and that becomes its own task — a self-sustaining process. All that is left for us after that is living meaningfully, so that the writing has a medium to express through. Some weird wavy light packet.

Helping Yourself First

So it pushed me to seek out other experiences, other meaningful lives that people have gone through. Some of them you could never experience yourself, but you can still learn from them separately to their true lived experience. There were several impactful stories. Randy Pausch, living with a terminal diagnosis and finding the meaning he sought out while expressing what he wanted for his kids and for everyone who wasn’t terminally ill. D’Angelo, an artistic mind shunted away by a country-sized number of individuals sexualising him, and through the lens of hundreds of years of oppression, then returning to show that nothing can prevent the beauty of his music or of him. And, of course, Kendrick Lamar, who was the final push that got me to write any of this down.

There are so many others, and they all tie to one important concept. None of these people asked anyone else how to build their own purposeful life. They were predisposed to it, and their circumstances made it all the more beautiful. They chose to live a beautiful life because it is in their nature, and it made some of the most meaningful mediums I have experienced and that many others could experience too. Each of them chose to help themselves so that they could help others, and I had to find my own moment for that, however small it may be by comparison. Because you live not only for yourself, but for everyone who interacts with you. Every person who passes you by, for however long in life, experiences some degree of the work you have put into yourself. They will recognise the effort, because it shows in how you interact, what you talk about, and the reason you had for meeting them in the first place. Be willing to share that with others, both to learn from them and to share the beauty they may resonate with.

Shouting into the Void

No matter how much effort you give towards other people, not everyone shares the qualities that give them purpose. Nor can you expect them to; they will only have got however far in life they have had the freedom to achieve. Lots of people will eventually learn to live meaningfully, because our world is designed to support people who believe in their work, but not everyone will. There are places for busy bees and workers, and that lifestyle is meaningful in its own way too. It is not self-serving, nor egocentric, and it does give back to everyone — given a working moral compass, of course. All we can do is show the effort that can be made and watch the effect trickle through the people we meet. We shout into the void and hope the effect echoes.

It is becoming harder for the next generation to exist nowadays, because of how much they have to worry about. Personally, I do believe that we solve problems to create the ability to worry about more problems in the future; if we have more to worry about, we have more problems to solve. However, we are forcing too many problems onto the next generation. AI, global warming, market instability, money-hungry country officials, geopolitical warfare, and so many more. While I believe mine, the next, and the next generation will handle it, there is still a set time limit on some of these. With that much to worry about, living purposefully becomes something completely outside of the picture. Less individuality, fewer important stories needing to be told, less societal development, and more keeping your head above water. It will become so hard to exist that everyone will be attempting to stay alive instead of living, let alone living with meaning.

Which concludes my thoughts on the topic for now. I want to look back on this feeling embarrassed, but contemplative. These are definitely some embarrassing thoughts to share, but someone will resonate with them and learn from them too. Since I started writing this, I have started at my first research gig that has truly interested me, supported by people who believe in the work that I’m doing. The feeling is second to none, and I hope that others can find that feeling too.

It may be a dull ending, but, hey, we’re talking about real life here, not some story.
entry.summary: What To Pimp A Butterfly, Kierkegaard, and a failing startup taught me about choosing to live with intention.

entry.title: Least Squares from 4 Angles
entry.content:
This topic was not one I expected to misunderstand so much. For a topic in Machine Learning, Least Squares is one of the fundamentals by far. However, it has more nuance and interoperable techniques that I’ve touched upon prior.

For this post, I’ll approach Least Squares from 1 angle, to do that we need to explore the Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse.

The motivation for the Pseudoinverse is best understood geometrically before tackling the mathematics. Consider first a matrix A:

\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]

This is a rectangular matrix that has column vectors \(v_1 \text{ and } v_2\) which define the column space (space defined by any linear combination of them). Defining the linear combination of them in this way we can understand the column space as a plane containing the region describable with them. The resulting graph looks as such!

This is a unitary portion of the overall column space for simplicity, but it spans in all directions achievable by their linear combination. Feel free to play around with this yourself. Remember that this describes the column space because it is the vectors defined by the columns of matrix A.

Now, any point defined in the column space is easily projected with the pseudoinverse of matrix A back to where it would have lied on the 3D graph axes known so well! As seen in the image prior, I’ve defined a point in that space right at the centre of the column space of a half combination of both column vectors. The pseudoinverse of A is non-trivial but it is,

\[A^{+} = \begin{pmatrix} 5.61218077\text{e-}17 & 1.53846154\text{e-}01 & 2.30769231\text{e-}01 \\ 3.33333333\text{e-}01 & -5.12820513\text{e-}02 & -7.69230769\text{e-}02 \end{pmatrix},\]

Not exactly the prettiest, but it does result in a known location for the half point in A’s column space, directly at point (0.5, 0.5) luckily (or mayhaps not luck)!

The point of contention here is that an inverse for this case was only easy because the point was described in a square portion of the matrix that we needed to consider. Non-square inverse matrices are not exactly a real concept, so we fill in the gap by introducing the Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse, which happens to be exactly what was used to produce the non-square inverse matrix seen prior.

To continue on the geometric understanding of the motivation, we were lucky enough to have a point described in the column space which consists of exactly 0 elements defined outside of a square portion of that matrix. If we had a point slightly above the surface, without the pseudoinverse it would be impossible to generate a description of it in the column-space of A. And that is effectively all but 2-dimensions accounted for by A, so there’s a lot of space missing and lots of possible points that we miss! To visualise this, here is a 2D example of two points, one lying on the surface, another lying outside the surface.

Here, there are two lines defining a 1-dimensional space where 2-dimensions can be described. The green point lies in the plane and is easily defined by the square components of the matrix. The red point lies outside the plane and relies on a column space description that extends to the second dimension, so an additional matrix component needs to define the value. The red point respectively gets projected into column space roughly above the centre between the green point and the end of the blue vector.

Now for the mathematical intuition, consider a rectangular matrix A and its SVD,

\[A = U \Sigma V^T,\]

as we showed in the previous post, the matrices U and V are square individually, but not in combination. The property that we want the pseudoinverse to hold is this,

\[A^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^T,\]

now is where we consider a goal to help us approach a definition, a sort of definition by characterisation. The goal is to find the pseudoinverse of course, but why we’re here in the first place is to understand Least Squares! That is minimising x for,

\[||Ax - b||,\]

where A is our matrix that is not of equal size, b is some point in basis space, and x is the value we’re looking to minimise. We start by defining two terms,

\[c = U^T b,\] \[z = V^T x.\]

V forms an orthonormal set so it follows that,

\[x = Vz \rightarrow ||x|| = ||z||,\]

therefore,

\[Ax = U\Sigma z,\]

and

\[||Ax - b|| = ||\Sigma z - c||.\]

Which reduces the problem to a diagonal problem, because \(\Sigma\) is diagonal. A search over a diagonal only cares about the rank r, resulting in,

\[||\Sigma z - c||^2 = \sum_{i=1}^r (\sigma_i z_i - c_i)^2 + \sum_{i=r+1}^M c_i^2.\]

Now because we’re minimising a Least Squares problem, this results in the term by term component,

\[\sigma_i z_i - c_i = 0 \rightarrow z_i = \frac{c_i}{\sigma_i}.\]

Despite this solution for z being optimal, we have too many options of the fraction definition. To pick the best one, we need to pick the point of the column space closest to the origin, which looks like,

\[||z||^2 = \sum_{i\leq r} z_i^2 + \sum_{i > r} z_i^2.\]

Which drives each component to 0, for every \(i > r\). What this means is that we define every component up to the base of the column space, after which nothing! In other words, this describes \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\), so x becomes,

\[x = V \Sigma^+ U^T b.\]

Which holds for every b so the operator that produces the best x is,

\[A^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^T.\]

What an interesting result! Randy Pausch would be proud of showing you both head fakes and actually going both directions at the same time. What we’ve done here has been coming in with the goal of understanding the Least Squares, but needing to define the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse and using both as stepping stones for each other to solve each; despite the pseudoinverse being naturally harder to derive from first principles.

Conclusion

This is probably the best approach you can take to understand both topics at once. I highly recommend readers derive from first principles, the Least Squares scenario via algebra, geometry, SVD, and probability. If you need hints, the topics of my two prior posts should give you enough headway. Also if you want some spare reading, that little mention I put in of Prof. Pausch is a great place to look, he felt like a modern-day Feynman! But maybe that is just a hint that most professors in our field have lots to say, just only a few have or had a platform to share it. Regardless, check out The Last Lecture!

And here’s a boring Least Squares graph, because there can only be space for one cool topic like the pseudoinverse!
entry.summary: Covering Least Squares solutions from the goal of describing the Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse.

entry.title: Singular Value Decomposition & A Coda for Principal Component Analysis

link.title: Singular Value Decomposition & A Coda for Principal Component Analysis

entry.content:
The connecting component between Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is the eigendecomposition. Principal component analysis requires keeping the top-k eigenvectors for reconstruction of the maximal information components. We can study the effect of this with a Gaussian.

Following on from the previous post, we used a covariance matrix to define conditionally dependent multivariate Gaussians. The covariance matrix can be thought of as a set of operations, a rotation, followed by scaling, finishing off with a final rotation. This looks like,

\[X = U \Sigma V^T,\]

for a given matrix X, the rotation components \(U\) and \(V\), with scaling \(\Sigma\). To relate to eigendecomposition, we consider a symmetric Positive SemiDefinite (PSD) matrix M,

\[M = X^T X,\]

where X is not necessarily square, but M is. Substituting in the SVD for X and eliminating variables results in,

\[X^T X = V \Sigma^2 V^T,\] \[X X^T = U \Sigma^2 U^T.\]

These equations are eigendecompositions themselves for the left and right eigenvectors, so the singular values of X are,

\[\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(X^T X)},\]

or the square roots of the non-zero eigenvalues of \(X^T X\) (equivalently \(XX^T\)). Therefore, the columns of \(U\) are eigenvectors of \(XX^T\) and the columns of \(V\) are eigenvectors of \(X^T X\).

The link between SVD and eigendecomposition allows PCA to perform a low-rank execution of decomposition for simpler operations. By taking the high dimensional dataset that PCA receives, and reducing to the axes with maximal variance, we retain the most information. With Gaussian covariance descriptions, the eigenvectors corresponded to ellipsoidal directions. Meaning that we collapse the meaningful information because it is easy to reproduce and it corresponds to a majority of the overall feature.

Low-Rank and Truncated SVD

To avoid hand-waving completely, I’ll revisit the low-rank concept for SVD. To begin, the reduced SVD assumes that for any SVD there are columns in U whose corresponding singular values are zero, so they contribute nothing to the reconstruction. Specifically for \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(m \ge n\),

\[U \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n},\]

we can define the reduced SVD as,

\[\tilde{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, \tilde{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, \tilde{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}.\]

This reduces the number of operations total that we need to perform. The rank of the matrix is then defined as the number of non-zero diagonal elements in \(\Sigma\). This brings another question in mind. Because there are certain columns of the matrices that we don’t need, can we take only the top-k elements from the decomposition for reconstruction?

To the machine learner, this is obviously PCA, and it directly follows that taking the top-k is an information preserving operation. But why is this? The matrix we consider is the eigendecomposition for simplicity, the diagonal elements are the eigenvalues and we get their retrieved eigenvectors from the other matrices. By considering a low-rank representation of the decomposition, we are taking only the first few eigenvalues, which means that the eigenvectors along other dimensions are zero-ed out. We order the eigenvalues based on maximal variance so that they describe the largest change. This top-k component procedure we perform to retain the eigenvectors which describe the principal information, by ordering based on variance. Therefore, PCA takes the decomposition to reduce the amount of information in a feature dataset, by describing maximal variance in the eigendecomposition.

Conclusion

We found out here exactly why PCA is related to eigendecomposition by the connection of eigendecomposition to SVD. PCA uses the low-rank description of a decomposition to retain maximally varying information in the eigenbasis. That’s the sum of everything we did here, just in a shorter form!
entry.summary: Deriving the relationship between SVD to eigendecomposition and their relations to PCA.

entry.title: Multivariate Gaussian PDFs
entry.content:
Gaussian probability density functions (PDFs) provide a new domain to understand 3-dimensional information using Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023). This technique, influenced by Neural Radiance Fields (Mildenhall et al., 2020), opened up deep learning techniques without the high compute barrier of the neural network representation.

Here I derive the basic properties of multivariate gaussians from fundamentals.

1D Gaussian PDF

The 1D Gaussian PDF is of the form,

\[p(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right),\]

where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation (\(\sigma^2\) the variance), controlling the spread of the gaussian simultaneously with the peak height, and \(\mu\) is the mean. This equation is alternatively a normal distribution and describes a standard probability distribution found across a variety of statistical scenarios.

2D Gaussian PDF for Independent Variables

A logical next step is how to define the Gaussian PDF in 2D; if we can define a Gaussian PDF in 2D then we can define an N-dimensional Gaussian PDF. We start off from the case of independent variables, which is just a resulting product of Gaussian PDFs,

\[p(x_1, x_2) = p(x_1) \cdot p(x_2) = \frac{1}{2 \pi \sigma_1 \sigma_2} \exp\left( -\frac{(x_1 - \mu_1)^2}{2 \sigma_1^2} - \frac{(x_2 - \mu_2)^2}{2 \sigma_2^2} \right),\]

with two independent variances and means. The resulting Gaussian PDF is allegorically a series of concentric ellipses with increasing distance between them. Then, let \(x = [x_1, x_2]\) and \(\mu = [\mu_1, \mu_2]\) and we rewrite the equation,

\[p(x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{2 \pi |A|^{1/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^T A^{-1} (x - \mu)}{2} \right),\]

where

\[A = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_2^2 \end{pmatrix}\]

is the covariance matrix in this independent case (note \(\lvert A \rvert^{1/2} = \sigma_1 \sigma_2\), so the prefactor agrees with the product form above). Its diagonal entries scale the two axes independently, so the level sets of \(p\) are axis-aligned ellipses — circles when \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\).

2D Gaussian PDF for Dependent Variables

Here we consider the exponent; its form is

\[-\frac{(x - \mu)^T A^{-1} (x - \mu)}{2}.\]

The missing piece of \(A\) is the covariance between the variables. We extend the matrix to include those off-diagonal dependence components. The covariance between \(x_1, x_2\) is

\[\text{cov}[x_1, x_2] = \mathbb{E}[(x_1 - \mu_1)(x_2 - \mu_2)],\]

the expectation of the product between the centred variable components. The covariance matrix can therefore be defined as,

\[\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \text{var}(x_1) & \text{cov}(x_1, x_2) \\ \text{cov}(x_2, x_1) & \text{var}(x_2) \end{pmatrix},\]

where the off-diagonal entries \(\text{cov}(x_1, x_2) = \text{cov}(x_2, x_1)\) are equal because covariance is symmetric by definition. The resulting PDF is,

\[p(x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{2 \pi |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)}{2} \right).\]

Geometrically, the off-diagonal terms rotate the level sets away from the coordinate axes — the ellipses tilt in the direction of correlation.

ND Gaussian PDF for Dependent Variables

The generalisation to \(N\) variables follows the same pattern. \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) keeps variances along the diagonal and fills the off-diagonals with covariances; the vectors \(x, \mu \in \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N\) simply grow in length. In the independent case the prefactor is a product of 1D normalisers,

\[\prod_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma_i^2}} = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{N/2} \prod_i \sigma_i},\]

which generalises to \(1 / ((2 \pi)^{N/2} \lvert \Sigma \rvert^{1/2})\) in the dependent case (note \(\lvert \Sigma \rvert = \prod_i \sigma_i^2\) when \(\Sigma\) is diagonal, recovering the product form). The resulting equation is

\[p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{N/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)}{2} \right).\]

Marginals of Joint Gaussian Distributions

We now move on with deriving conditional probabilities.

2D Independent Variables

This is the simplest case, solved logically or mathematically. The equation for the gaussian is a density function, so we can integrate over one variable,

\[p(x_1) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x_1, x_2) \,dx_2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x_1) p(x_2) \,dx_2 = p(x_1) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x_2) \,dx_2,\]

where the factorisation is allowed because the PDFs are independent. The result is just \(p(x_1)\) because the area under a gaussian PDF is 1 (the total probability). Alternatively, you can notice that the marginal, if not conditioned on any other variable, results in an independent PDF.

2D Dependent Variables

For the dependent case, we consider the equation from before,

\[p(x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{2 \pi |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)}{2} \right).\]

The conditional probability can be found from

\[p(x_2 | x_1) = \frac{p(x_1, x_2)}{p(x_1)},\]

where the denominator is the familiar 1D Gaussian PDF. Let \(\rho = \text{cov}(x_1, x_2) / (\sigma_1 \sigma_2)\) be the correlation, so that \(\lvert \Sigma \rvert = \sigma_1^2 \sigma_2^2 (1 - \rho^2)\) and the joint quadratic form expands as

\[(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu) = \frac{1}{1 - \rho^2}\left[\frac{(x_1 - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{2 \rho (x_1 - \mu_1)(x_2 - \mu_2)}{\sigma_1 \sigma_2} + \frac{(x_2 - \mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2}\right].\]

Completing the square in \(x_2\) separates it into a piece depending on \(x_2\) and one that does not,

\[(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu) = \frac{[(x_2 - \mu_2) - \rho (\sigma_2 / \sigma_1)(x_1 - \mu_1)]^2}{\sigma_2^2 (1 - \rho^2)} + \frac{(x_1 - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2}.\]

The second term, together with the matching factor in the joint’s normalisation, is exactly \(p(x_1)\), which cancels in the ratio. What remains is itself a 1D Gaussian in \(x_2\),

\[p(x_2 | x_1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma_2^2 (1 - \rho^2)}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x_2 - \mu_{2|1})^2}{2 \sigma_{2|1}^2} \right),\]

with conditional mean and variance

\[\mu_{2|1} = \mu_2 + \rho \frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}(x_1 - \mu_1), \qquad \sigma_{2|1}^2 = \sigma_2^2 (1 - \rho^2).\]

So observing \(x_1\) shifts the mean of \(x_2\) along the regression line and shrinks its variance by a factor of \((1 - \rho^2)\). In the general \(N\)-D case the same algebra (block-matrix inversion) gives

\[p(x_b | x_a) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu_b + \Sigma_{ba} \Sigma_{aa}^{-1}(x_a - \mu_a),\; \Sigma_{bb} - \Sigma_{ba} \Sigma_{aa}^{-1} \Sigma_{ab}\bigr).\]

Conclusion

This concludes the overview on multivariate Gaussian PDFs, there’s many applications of Gaussian’s so understanding their basics is very important. If you are reading this and on your path to begin your academic career, I highly recommend deriving this yourself and coding up visualisations to help you understand the way the components interact.
